## Overview

The Hup, also known as Hupda, Hup, Hupd'äh, or Húpd’əh, are an Amazonian Indigenous people living in Brazil and Colombia. Their territory lies between the Tiquié and Papuri rivers, tributaries of the Vaupés, in Brazil’s state of Amazonas and Colombia’s Department of Vaupés. They live in approximately 35 villages, or local groups, with an estimated total of 1500 individuals. The Hup language belongs to the Naduhup language family. Hupda life is organized around forest-based mobility, hunting, small local groups, patrilinear clans, and relationships with Tukanoan, Desana, Tuyuka, and Tariano peoples. Their cultural importance in the sources lies especially in their knowledge of forest resources, their distinctive social organization, their shamanic medical system, and the linguistic and ritual practices through which clan membership and relationships are maintained.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

They do mention dietary restrictions associated with healing practices: a patient may be required to abstain from cooked meats, salt, and peppers, avoid touching menstruating women, and observe sexual abstinence for a prescribed period.

### Architecture

Hupda villages are small and do not consist of fixed villages or permanent camps in the usual sense. A local group, normally called a *hayam*, is associated with a stream, its source, or a clearing. The terms *-deh* mean “stream,” *-nuh* means “head,” referring to the source of the stream, and *-buk* indicates that a group stays in a clearing. The names of local places are the names of the small streams where groups draw water.

A local group may join another group or divide itself between two others, and its movements may change from one year to the next. Some groups remain in one location for years while still treating the settlement as temporary. The sources state that clearings are places where houses are found, and that they are also special places for ceremonies and socializing with other Hupda.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They describe the *kakah*, the hearth group, as the smallest unit of production and consumption. It may consist of a nuclear family or include mothers-in-law, orphaned nephews, and widowed uncles. The sources also mention a *cuia*, a gourd made from the fruit of *Lagenaria vulgaris*, used by the shaman during healing recitations.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Clan names are socially significant: each clan has a set of five to seven proper names for each sex, and receiving a clan name through the *bi’ìd - hàt* naming ritual makes a newborn child a member of the clan.

## Music & performance

They do describe several ritual and ceremonial practices.

Each clan has a specific set of ceremonies and stories. The most important ceremony of a clan is the one that transmits its name. It is generally performed by the oldest male in the clan who has a direct family relationship with the person receiving the name, or by the father’s father if he is still alive. This naming ceremony is called *bi’ìd - hàt*. The name of an ancestor is changed and given to a newborn child; the name is used in everyday life and is not secret.

The Hupda also practice *Dabucuri* and celebrate *Jurupari*, traditions described in the sources as common among the clans of the Alto Rio Negro region. The Hupda maintain their own *kapi-vaiyá*. The *pä’* or dabucuri celebrations take place between local groups rather than between clans. These celebrations therefore help connect local groups within the wider Hupda social world.

Healing is also performed through spoken ritual. The term *bi’id* covers rituals ranging from a basic blessing to complex magic. *Bi’in*, translated in the source as “breath” or “blow,” refers to the shaman’s recitation of formulas in a susurration of words, with a *cuia* near his mouth.

## Dance & theatre

They state that clearings are places for ceremonies and socializing, and that *Dabucuri* celebrations occur between local groups.

## Festivals & rituals

They do describe ceremonies connected with clans, naming, healing, and inter-group relations.

The *bi’ìd - hàt* is a naming ritual through which an ancestor’s name is given to a newborn child. Each clan has a specific set of names for men and women, and names are repeated according to the birth order of ancestors. The first-born son receives his grandfather’s name, while subsequent boys may receive the names of younger brothers of the grandfather. The ritual establishes the child as a member of the clan and gives access to knowledge, privileges, and responsibilities associated with that clan.

The Hupda practice *Dabucuri*, called *pä’* in the Hupda material presented by the source, between local groups. They also celebrate *Jurupari* and maintain their own *kapi-vaiyá*.

Healing ceremonies are called *bi’in dóhoité*. They invoke the forces of the forest to strengthen the *hawäg*, the vital energy located in the chest, and reduce the influence of the *b’atub’*, associated with a shadow or personal ghost. The patient may need to remain lying down for most of the prescribed period and follow a special diet.

## Foodways

The Hupda are described as hunters who know the forest intimately. Unlike their neighbors, who practice agriculture extensively, they do not work in agriculture. Hupda groups hunt within territories associated with streams and periodically leave those territories to hunt or visit villages of in-laws. Such visits are important to the regeneration of renewable resources in the areas where local groups live.

They do mention cured meat and fish in the context of relations with Tukanoan villages: Tukanoan people sometimes visit Hupda villages to collect such foods, while Hupda people may work in Tukanoan settlements in exchange for outside resources.

Food also appears in the medical system. One category of illness is attributed to prepared poisons mixed into food and drink; these illnesses can be cured if the source and sender are known. During healing, patients generally abstain from cooked meats, salt, and peppers. Avoiding cooked meat is therefore described as part of a therapeutic diet rather than as a general food rule. The sources also state that cocoa, tobacco, paricá, and *kapi* are used by the shaman in relation to dreaming and the diagnosis of illness. The Hup terms given are *pu’úk* for cocoa, *hunt* for tobacco, and *seâheak* for paricá.

## Oral tradition & literature

Hupda oral tradition is closely connected with clan identity, naming, cosmology, and healing. Each clan knows a specific set of ceremonies and stories, and this knowledge is shared among its members. The *bi’ìd - hàt* transmits an ancestor’s name to a newborn child and establishes the child’s place within the clan hierarchy.

The Hupda cosmology describes several worlds superimposed on one another. The terrestrial world is called *s’áh*, and the human body is *sáp*. Toward the East is *wedó ip mòy*, the house of the father of the sun and moon. At the western end is *s’áh-tút*, from which the river waters flow and where cold is found. Other worlds lie below the earth and waters, including *s’àk e o pèj mòy*, the world of the umari and the spirits, while worlds above include *K’èg-teh mòy*, *wero-meh mòy*, and *wã-mòy*. *K’èg-teh* is described as a principal hero and creator of earthly beings, stars, birds, and vultures.

The stories of *K’èg-teh* provide meanings for events occurring in the human world and are used in the medical system.

## Language & religion

Hup is one of the four Naduhup languages and is spoken by Hupda people living between Colombia and the Brazilian state of Amazonas. The sources give approximately 1500 speakers. Hupda children learn Hup as their first language, and the language is described as not seriously endangered in the cited account. Hup is most closely related to Yuhup, followed by Dâw and then Nadëb. Hup and Yuhup share more than 90% of their basic vocabularies.

The language has been described in vocabulary lists, dictionaries, and Patience Epps’s *A Grammar of Hup*, written in 2005 and updated in 2008. Hup is highly agglutinative and has a frequent subject-object-verb order. The sources describe a word-accent system with rising and high tones, and they state that there is no general Hup lexeme or morpheme meaning “no.”

Hupda cosmology includes multiple worlds inhabited by mythological beings in the forms of animals, fruits, and energies. The body contains *hawäg*, a vital energy associated with the heart, and *b’atub’*, associated with a shadow or personal ghost. The medical system is shamanic. The shaman, or *bi’id-ih*, uses plants in dreams and trance to diagnose illness, while curing ceremonies seek to strengthen *hawäg* and reduce the influence of *b’atub’*.
